transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-09-14
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes
Attendees: Evan Brooks (Redwood AE), Sofia Martinez (Redwood SE), Priya Anand (CTO - Halcyon), Liam O'Neill (Platform), Chen Wu (SRE), Asha Verma (ML Infra), Raj Patel (Security - joined late)

Summary: quick technical workshop to triage persistent p99 spikes seen in Halcyon's inference stacks. Focus areas: edge proxy / Envoy hop amplification, TLS/TCP overhead at the edge, streaming vs unary (non-streaming) behavior, and quantization-induced jitter. Agreed to run targeted multi-region benchmarks and exchange prompt sets + KV hot-key list.

Topics: edge proxies, VPC peering, MTU and path MTU effects, TLS handshake cost, gRPC streaming vs unary, chunking & SSE, KV cache sharding, hot key mitigation, quantization (int8) dequant overhead, batching tradeoffs, p95/p99 SLOs

Transcript:
[00:00] Evan Brooks: Okay, thanks everyone for joining. we have about an hour, um we want to get into the p99 tail stuff you flagged, Priya. Sofia will lead the bench plan, i'm on notes and follow-ups.
[00:15] Priya Anand: yeah thanks, Evan. we've been seeing these intermittent p99 spikes on our chat endpoint, median is fine p50's 30-35 ms but the p99 jumps to 480ms in bursts, sometimes up to 700. it's not every hour, it's kind of microburst-y.
[00:32] Sofia Martinez: okay, cool. first quick Q: are those measurements from hosted Redwood or dedicated infra?
[00:39] Liam O'Neill: entirely on our dedicated cluster in GCE region us-west1, we run a Envoy sidecar at the edge and also an internal edge proxy in front of the cluster (we call it edge-proxy).
[00:52] Chen Wu: to add, we have VPC peering to the model serving VMs. sometimes we see extra RTT when peering flipovers happen.
[00:59] Sofia Martinez: got it — so multiple network hops before the request hits the GPU host. that can amplify latency variance, especially for short requests. couple things to check: TLS handshakes, keepalive settings, and whether your edge-proxy is doing buffering or connection pooling correctly.
[01:18] Priya Anand: the edge-proxy is a custom nginx-ish thing. we use TLS passthrough to Envoy, but sometimes we terminate at the edge for internal calls. not always consistent.
[01:29] Evan Brooks: note: tls termination strategy matters because each termination can add up — CPU for crypto and also extra socket hops.
[01:35] [00:60] Sofia Martinez: (laughs) i say 00:60, sorry, bad habits. moving on: streaming vs unary — are you using streaming tokens back to callers or waiting for final response?
[01:45] Asha Verma: we implemented streaming for the chat UI but fallback to non-streaming for some background batch scoring flows. interestingly the p99 spikes are mostly on the streaming path.
[01:55] Sofia Martinez: that's consistent with head-of-line amplification — streaming keeps connections open longer which affects concurrency and also interaction with prefix/KV caching. if you have many concurrent streaming conns, tokens interleave and proxies may hit per-connection buffers.
[02:12] Liam O'Neill: we also saw larger packets due to SSE chunking we do, maybe that's triggering path MTU issues — packets get fragmented and retransmits cause spikes.
[02:20] Sofia Martinez: yes MTU fragmentation + TCP retransmit will show up as p99. check your path MTU discovery and edge MTU. Also if the edge-proxy is reassembling and then re-chunking that compounds latency.
[02:33] Priya Anand: can quantization cause jitter? we moved to int8 on one model and saw slightly worse tail in some cases, while average token cost dropped.
[02:41] Sofia Martinez: possible. int8 quantization reduces compute but adds dequant/quant ops on the CPU/GPU boundary on every token generation step depending on runtime. if the runtime isn't fully fused for the quantized kernels, you can get small per-token overhead that hurts short requests and tail.
[02:58] Chen Wu: our serving runtime is a mix — some model variants are fused and some run through a less optimized path. are there suggestions for identifying that?
[03:06] Sofia Martinez: we usually run a kernel profiler and compare token latency with and without KV prefix. also run a micro-bench: single-token loop with the quantized model to surface per-token jitter. Redwood can run this too in a controlled bench.
[03:20] Evan Brooks: we'll add that micro-bench as an action item.

[03:30] [03:30] Sofia Martinez: another big source is KV cache hot keys. if a few keys map to the same shard / GPU and that GPU experiences transient load, you'll see amplified p99 for all requests hitting those keys. are your KV shards per GPU?
[03:46] Liam O'Neill: yes, we shard per-GPU. our top 10 keys are 60% of traffic, not surprising.
[03:53] Sofia Martinez: okay that's a classic hot-shard. mitigation options: add consistent hashing with replica reads, increase hot-key cache capacity, or add local LRU at the edge to absorb spikes. Redwood also has prefix-level caching that can be pinned to avoid cross-GPU reads.
[04:10] Priya Anand: we tried LRU at the edge but it wasn't consistent on failover. how do you suggest making that robust?
[04:16] Sofia Martinez: one pattern: keep small local edge cache as best-effort for read-through, but always fallback to a central KV with rate-limited async refreshes. avoids serving stale critical results but absorbs bursts. also consider TTLs and negative caching for missing keys.
[04:30] Evan Brooks: network hop count math example: if you have client -> edge-proxy -> envoy -> redis-kv -> model-host, that's 4-5 serialized handoffs. each hop adds not just RTT but queuing variance. eliminating a hop often reduces p99 more than optimizing a single hop by 10%.
[04:46] Chen Wu: interesting — we can collapse envoy+edge-proxy in some traffic routes, but worried about losing security controls.
[04:54] Raj Patel: (joined) hi apologies for delay, from security perspective we can allow passthrough with mutual TLS if audit logs remain intact. want to see the exact flow chart.
[05:04] Sofia Martinez: good to have you. note: mTLS passthrough and audit logs are supported — we'll share config recommendations.

[05:20] [05:20] Sofia Martinez: streaming vs non-streaming — another nuance: gRPC streaming tends to have smaller message sizes but more frequent I/O, while unary can pack larger payloads and benefit from single-send optimizations. depending on where your bottleneck is (net vs compute) one will outperform the other on tail.
[05:38] Liam O'Neill: we use gRPC unary for scoring and gRPC bidi for interactive chat. maybe we should standardize.
[05:44] Sofia Martinez: benchmarking is the only safe way. in our experience, for chat with many short turns, streaming gives perceived latency improvement but can increase server-side p99 when combined with small batch sizes and high concurrency.

[06:00] Evan Brooks: let's talk about batching — especially the continuous batching patterns. what's your current max batch window?
[06:07] Asha Verma: we set it to 25ms.
[06:10] Sofia Martinez: small batch windows reduce latency but reduce batching efficiency, and under low load you get small batches which mainly affect throughput not tail. big thing for tail is head-of-line blocking inside batch merges — if a slow request joins a batch it delays others. Redwood supports dynamic batch shaping and early release for urgent requests.
[06:30] Priya Anand: early release — can you explain more? we've seen a single long context request hold a GPU and delay others.
[06:38] Sofia Martinez: early release lets the runtime detect requests with long expected generation and evict non-critical tokens from the batch or spawn a secondary execution path for high-latency requests. it's not perfect but helps p99 for short requests.

[06:55] [06:55] Chen Wu: kernel selection also came up — you mentioned fused attention. is it true that fused kernels can both shrink p50 and p99?
[07:02] Sofia Martinez: yes if well-implemented. fused kernels reduce per-token overhead and memory copies. but when quantized kernels are missing for a path, we fallback to unfused kernels that spike. so model variant management and pinned quantization profiles are critical.
[07:19] Evan Brooks: action item: timebox a model-variant rollout with staged traffic. do canary then 10% then 50% then full.

[07:30] [07:30] Sofia Martinez: also worth checking TCP connection reuse. some of the spikes correlate with connection churn — are proxies reusing keepalive or dialing fresh connections to backend hosts?
[07:41] Liam O'Neill: we have short keepalive on the edge to avoid idle sockets, maybe too aggressive.
[07:46] Sofia Martinez: increase keepalive and tune accept queues — ephemeral sockets cost slow-start and handshake time which affects short requests heavily.

[07:58] Priya Anand: about observability — what metrics should we instrument to tie p99 to network hops vs compute?
[08:05] Sofia Martinez: instrument per-hop p95/p99 latencies (client->edge, edge->envoy, envoy->model), socket-level metrics (handshake time, rtt, retransmits), per-GPU queue depth, and per-shard KV latency. also correlate with system metrics like CPU steal, GPU stalls, and NIC interrupts.
[08:24] Chen Wu: we have per-host tracing but not end-to-end traces. will enable trace context to track cross-host path.

[08:36] [08:36] Sofia Martinez: we also discussed TLS offload: if your edge can do hardware TLS offload it reduces CPU jitter. but be mindful of added hop if offload box is an extra network step. it's tradeoff.

[08:52] Evan Brooks: curious: have you ruled out hypervisor scheduling or noisy neighbors on the host?
[08:58] Liam O'Neill: we run dedicated VMs per-customer but occasionally burst into shared infra for batch. some spikes line up with batch windows.
[09:05] Sofia Martinez: that will show as CPU steal — correlate the p99 windows with host-level steal and background batch schedule. also check firmware NIC drivers; we've seen bad drivers cause incast and retransmit storms.

[09:20] [09:20] Sofia Martinez: let's sketch an experiment plan — short list: 1) isolate network hops by collapsing edge proxy for a subset of traffic and compare p99; 2) run quantized vs fp16 micro-bench to measure per-token overhead; 3) run KV hot-key replica test to see effect of local caching; 4) vary streaming vs unary under controlled concurrency; 5) collect full traces for two spike windows.
[09:46] Priya Anand: sounds good. for collapsing edge proxy we might need security signoff which Raj can help with.
[09:53] Raj Patel: yes we'll need to review the risk but feasible under controlled canary.

[10:05] [10:05] Sofia Martinez: benchmark details — we'll produce a spreadsheet with columns: timestamp, request_id, route, request_size, tokens_generated, server-side per-hop latencies, kv-lookup-time, kernel-path (fused/unfused), quantized? yes/no, batch_id, gpu_queue_depth. please include your real traffic distribution.
[10:28] Liam O'Neill: we can provide logs and a small sample trace set. we'll sanitize sensitive info.

[10:40] Evan Brooks: on the quantization note — Redwood has a recommended int8 profile we can share; it's been tuned to avoid per-token dequant hot paths. but we need your prompt shapes to recommend a variant.
[10:53] Sofia Martinez: also watch out for non-deterministic serialization in your proxy — JSON streaming libraries can block if they do big internal copies.

[11:04] [11:04] Chen Wu: any advice on guarding against KV flash crowds during deploys?
[11:09] Sofia Martinez: yes, introduce circuit-breaker for KV reads falling back to slightly stale local cache under high load, and pre-warm caches during rollouts. also use token-bucket rate-limiting on read paths.

[11:22] Priya Anand: okay quick recap?
[11:24] Evan Brooks: recap: 1) run the five experiments Sofia listed; 2) Redwood (Sofia) will run micro-bench and multi-region p99 bench and share spreadsheet; 3) Halcyon provides request distribution, top keys and traces; 4) Raj reviews security plan for collapsing edge for a canary; 5) exchange quantization profiles and run small canary rollout.
[11:46] Sofia Martinez: i'll create the bench spreadsheet and push a small test harness. linking deck: https://redwood.example.com/decks/edge-hop-latency-workshop (note: internal link). benchmark spreadsheet template: https://redwood.example.com/benchmarks/halcyon-template (we'll upload results there).
[11:58] Priya Anand: great. thanks, everyone.
[12:02] Evan Brooks: thanks all. we'll follow up via email with next steps and schedule a 30-min check-in for results.
[12:10] (meeting ends)

Notes: occasional mis-transcriptions present; speaker labels may shift in a few lines. references to Envoy/Envoy config, MTU, TLS offload, and quant/kernel selection were discussed.
